lessons.title: Values and types
lessons.summary: Tell the four basic types apart and know which type a value has.

blocks.text: Every value has a **type**. The type decides what you are allowed to do with the value.
Python has four basic types that you will use all the time. You never write the type yourself: Python looks at how the value is written and knows.

blocks.caption: The four basic types

blocks.text: The quotes are what make a **str**. **5** is an int, **"5"** is a str and **5.0** is a float. They look alike on screen, but they are three different values that behave differently.

blocks.caption: **type()** tells you the type of any value:

blocks.text: Use **type()** whenever you are not sure what you are holding. It answers the question "what is this?".

blocks.caption: Same digits, different types, different results:

blocks.text: With numbers, **+** adds. With strings, **+** glues the text together. Mixing an int with a float gives a float.

blocks.why: **True** and **False** start with a capital letter. Lowercase **true** is just an unknown name, so Python raises a **NameError**.
Without quotes, Python thinks **Alice** is the name of a variable. Text always needs quotes.
**type()** gives back the type itself, not its name as text. Compared with the str **"int"** it is never equal, so the first version prints False. Compare with **int** without quotes.

blocks.text: A number inside quotes is text, not a number. **"7" + 1** is an error. You will see this again with **input()**, which always gives you text.

items: **int** for counting, **float** for measuring, **str** for text, **bool** for yes/no.
Quotes make a str: **"5"** is text.
A decimal point makes a float: **5.0** is a float.
**True** and **False** are written with a capital letter.

lessons.title: Variables and assignment
lessons.summary: Store values in variables, update them, and read an assignment the right way round.

blocks.text: **=** means "store the value on the right under the name on the left". It is not the equals sign from maths.
Python always works out the **right side first**. Then it stores the result under the name on the left. The name keeps that value until you store something else in it.
Storing a new value replaces the old one. Python does not remember the 17 any more.
Updating a variable

blocks.caption: Read it as: take the current x, add 1, store the result back in x.

blocks.text: **x = x + 1** is impossible in maths, but in Python it is one of the most common lines you will write. The right side uses the old value, and the result becomes the new value.

blocks.caption: A variable stores a value, not a formula:

blocks.text: When **b = a \* 3** ran, a was 2, so b got 6. Changing a later does not change b.

blocks.caption: Tracing it line by line: the value of each variable after each line

blocks.text: When code confuses you, trace it like this on paper: one row per line, one column per variable. It is the single most useful habit in this course.
Swapping two variables

blocks.code:
a = 1
b = 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)

blocks.why: After **a = b** the old value of a is gone, so **b = a** just copies b back into b. Swap with **a, b = b, a**, or save one value in a temporary variable first.

blocks.text: Naming rules

rows: Must not start with a digit
Upper and lower case are different

blocks.text: A name must have a value before you use it. Using a name that was never assigned raises a **NameError**.
Python runs your code from top to bottom. A line can only use names that earlier lines have already stored.

items: **=** stores. **==** compares (see the Conditions lesson).
The right side is worked out first, then stored.
A new assignment replaces the old value.
Swap with **a, b = b, a**.

lessons.title: input() and print()
lessons.summary: Read what the user types, convert it to a number when needed, and print results the way you want.

blocks.text: **input()** always gives you a **str**, even when the user types a number. Convert it with **int()** or **float()** before you do maths with it.
**input()** pauses the program, shows its prompt, waits until the user presses Enter, and then hands you exactly what they typed, as text.

blocks.caption: The user types 17, and this still crashes:
blocks.code:
age = input("Age? ")  # the user types 17
print(age + 1)
blocks.output: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

blocks.text: The user typed 17, but **age** holds the text **"17"**. Text plus a number is a **TypeError**. Convert first:

blocks.code:
age = int(input("Age? "))  # the user types 17
print(age + 1)

blocks.caption: Converting between types
rows: cuts off the decimals, does not round
int() cannot read a decimal point in text
the text is not a number at all

blocks.why: With a str, \* repeats the text, so typing 4 prints 44. Convert with **int()** to get 8.
Comparing the str **"20"** with the int **18** using **>=** is a **TypeError**. Convert the input as soon as you read it.

blocks.text: print()
**print()** shows its values on one line. Give it several values separated by commas and it puts a space between them, then ends the line.

blocks.code:
name = "Sam"
age = 20
print(name, "is", age)
print(name, age, sep="-")
print("no newline", end="")
print("!")

blocks.text: **sep=** changes what goes between the values (a space by default). **end=** changes what goes at the end (a new line by default).
f-strings

blocks.code:
name = "Sam"
age = 20
print(f"{name} will be {age + 1} next year")

blocks.text: Put an **f** before the quotes and write any expression inside **{ }**. Python works it out and turns it into text for you, so you do not need **str()**.

blocks.caption: Add **:.2f** inside the braces to show exactly 2 decimals:

blocks.why: **+** only joins a str to a str. Convert with **str()**, or use a comma: **print("Score:", 10)**, or use an f-string.

blocks.text: **print()** shows a value on the screen; it does not give one back. **x = print(5)** prints 5 and stores **None** in x.

items: **input()** gives a str. Always.
**int()** for whole numbers, **float()** for decimals.
Commas in **print()** add spaces; **+** does not.
f-strings convert values to text for you.

lessons.title: Arithmetic operators
lessons.summary: Use every arithmetic operator, predict whether a result is an int or a float, and use % and // for digits and even numbers.

blocks.text: **/** always gives a float. **//** gives the whole part, rounded down. **%** gives the remainder.
Even when a division comes out even, **/** gives a float: **6 / 3** is **2.0**, not **2**. Use **//** when you need an int.
Remainder tricks

items: **n % 2 == 0** means n is even; **n % 2 == 1** means n is odd.
**n % 10** is the last digit of n.
**n // 10** is n with its last digit removed.
**n % k == 0** means n is divisible by k.

blocks.text: Rounding down, also with negatives
**//** always rounds **down**, towards minus infinity. For a negative number that is not the same as cutting off the decimals: -3.5 rounds down to -4.
Worked example: the digits of a number

blocks.code:
n = 472
hundreds = n // 100
tens = n // 10 % 10
ones = n % 10
print(hundreds, tens, ones)
print(hundreds + tens + ones)

blocks.caption: Each digit with // and %

blocks.text: Order of operations
Power first, then multiplication and the divisions (**/**, **//** and **%**), then **+** and **-**. Use brackets whenever you are unsure.

blocks.why: Division happens before addition, so the first line computes a + (b / 2). Put the sum in brackets.
**^** is not the power operator in Python. It is a different operator you will not need here, and **5 ^ 2** gives 7, without any error. Power is two stars.

blocks.text: Shortcuts
**total += 5** is short for **total = total + 5**. The same shortcut works for every operator.
An int combined with a float always gives a float: **3 + 1.0** is **4.0**.

items: **/** always gives a float; **//** gives a whole number, rounded down.
**%** is the remainder: **n % 2 == 0** means even, **n % 10** is the last digit.
Power is two stars (\*\*), never **^**.
Power, then \* / // %, then + and -. Brackets when in doubt.

lessons.title: Built-in functions you use every day
lessons.summary: Call len, abs, round, min, max and the type functions, use what they give back, and avoid the classic calling mistakes.

blocks.text: A **function call** is a name followed by brackets: **len("hello")**. The values inside the brackets are the **arguments**. The function does its job and gives a value back, which you can print, store or use in a bigger calculation.

You have been calling functions since your first program: **print()**, **input()**, **int()** and **type()** are all built-in functions. Python has a small set of them that you will use in almost every program.

blocks.caption: Anatomy of a function call
rows: **( )**: they are what makes it a call

blocks.caption: The built-ins you will use most:
Built-in functions cheat sheet
rows: x rounded to a whole number (an int)

blocks.text: round() and the halves

A value exactly halfway between two whole numbers rounds to the **even** one: **round(2.5)** is 2 and **round(3.5)** is 4. Everything else rounds the way you expect. It surprises almost everyone, so remember it.
Using what a function gives back

blocks.code:
word = "banana"
n = len(word)
print(n * 2)
print(max(3, 8) + 1)
print(len(str(12345)))

blocks.text: A call can go anywhere a value can go: in a calculation, in an assignment, or inside another call. Nested calls are worked out **from the inside out**: **str(12345)** gives **"12345"**, then **len()** counts its 5 characters.
What goes wrong

blocks.caption: An argument of the wrong type is a **TypeError**:
blocks.output: TypeError: object of type 'int' has no len()

blocks.text: **len()** counts characters, and a number has no characters. Turn it into text first: **len(str(2026))** is 4.

blocks.why: Without brackets nothing is called. **name = input** only gives the function a second name, so print shows something like **<built-in function input>** instead of what the user typed.

**len = 3** replaces the built-in **len** with the number 3, so **len("abc")** turns into **3("abc")**: **TypeError: 'int' object is not callable**. Never name a variable **len**, **max**, **min**, **sum**, **str**, **int**, **list** or **input**.

blocks.text: **print()** shows a value; it does not give one back. If you want to use a result later, store what the function returns: **n = len(word)**, not **n = print(len(word))**.

items: A call is a name plus brackets; the brackets are not optional.
**len**, **abs**, **min**, **max**, **round** each give a value back. Use it, store it or print it.
Nested calls run from the inside out.
**round(2.5)** is 2: halves go to the even number.
Do not use built-in names as variable names.

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.summary: Index, slice and combine strings, use their methods, and know what a string will not let you do.

blocks.text: A string is a sequence of characters numbered from **0**. You can read any character, but you can never change one: strings are **immutable**.

blocks.caption: Indexes of "python": counting from the front and from the back

blocks.text: The last index is always **len(word) - 1**. Asking for **word[6]** is an **IndexError**. Negative indexes count from the end: **word[-1]** is the last character.
Slicing

**word[start:stop]** gives the characters from start up to, but **not including**, stop. Leave out start to begin at 0; leave out stop to go to the end. A third number is the step: **[::-1]** walks backwards, which reverses the string.
Slicing never raises an IndexError. **word[2:100]** simply stops at the end of the string.
Combining strings

blocks.code:
first = "Ada"
last = "Lovelace"
print(first + " " + last)
print("ha" * 3)
print("da" in first)

blocks.caption: What you can and cannot do with strings
rows: TypeError: you can only repeat by an int

blocks.text: Methods give you a new string

blocks.code:
name = "  Ada  "
clean = name.strip()
print(clean)
print(clean.upper())
print(clean.replace("A", "E"))
print("a,b,c".split(","))
print("banana".find("n"))

blocks.text: **strip()** removes spaces at both ends, **upper()** and **lower()** change case, **replace()** swaps text, **split()** cuts the string into a list, and **find()** gives the index of the first match (or -1).
Because strings are immutable, a method never changes the string you call it on. It returns a **new** string, so you have to store the result.

blocks.why: **name.upper()** returns "ADA", but nothing stores it, so the first version still prints ada.
You cannot change a character inside a string. Build a new string from pieces and store that instead.

blocks.text: Comparing strings

Strings compare character by character, like a dictionary, but **every capital letter comes before every small letter**. Digits in a string are characters too: **"10" < "9"** is True because **"1"** comes before **"9"**. Compare numbers as numbers: convert first.

items: Indexes start at **0**; the last one is **len(s) - 1**, or **-1**.
A slice leaves out its stop index.
**+** needs two strings; \* needs a string and an int.
Methods return a new string. Store it.

lessons.title: Booleans and if
lessons.summary: Write conditions with comparisons and and/or/not, and predict which branch of an if/elif/else runs.

blocks.text: **if** runs its block only when the condition is **True**. In an **if / elif / else** chain, only the **first** true branch runs.

blocks.caption: Comparisons give a bool

blocks.why: One **=** stores a value; two **==** compare. Using **=** in a condition is a **SyntaxError**.

blocks.text: 25 > 20 is True, so Python prints warm and skips the rest of the chain, even though 25 > 10 is also True. **else** runs only when no branch above it was True.

blocks.why: A score of 95 is also at least 50, so the first version prints pass and never reaches excellent. Put the strictest test first.

blocks.text: Separate **if** statements are all checked, one after another. An **elif** is only checked when everything above it in the chain was False.

blocks.why: Python spells it **elif**, one word. **else if** on one line is a **SyntaxError** (other languages allow it, Python does not).

blocks.text: and, or, not

blocks.code:
age = 20
has_ticket = False
print(age >= 18 and has_ticket)
print(age >= 18 or has_ticket)
print(not has_ticket)
print(0 < age < 30)

blocks.text: Python lets you chain comparisons: **0 < age < 30** means **0 < age and age < 30**.

blocks.why: Each side of **or** is its own condition. The text **"yes"** on its own counts as True, so the first version is always True.

blocks.text: The lesson **Combining conditions** goes deeper into **and**, **or** and **not**: truth tables, ranges, and why the order of the two sides can matter.
Indentation is the block
The indented lines belong to the **if**. The first line that is not indented is outside it, and it always runs.
Comparing different types

blocks.output:
False
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'

blocks.text: **==** between an int and a str is allowed and simply gives False. **<** between them is a **TypeError**. One more reason to convert **input()** first.
Every **if**, **elif** and **else** line ends with a colon, and the block under it is indented by 4 spaces.

items: **=** stores, **==** compares.
In an **if / elif / else** chain only the first True branch runs, so put the strictest test first.
**else** has no condition; it runs when nothing above it was True.
Indentation decides what is inside the **if**.

lessons.title: Combining conditions: and, or, not
lessons.summary: Combine conditions with and, or and not, write ranges correctly, and use short-circuiting to keep a check safe.

blocks.text: **and** is True only when **both** sides are True. **or** is True when **at least one** side is True. **not** turns True into False and False into True.

A single comparison answers one question, like **age >= 18**. Real decisions often need two: old enough **and** has a ticket; weekend **or** holiday. **and**, **or** and **not** combine conditions into one.

blocks.caption: The truth table: every combination

blocks.text: Read the table by columns: **and** has only one True row (both True); **or** has only one False row (both False). And **not True** is False, **not False** is True.

blocks.code:
age = 20
has_ticket = False
print(age >= 18 and has_ticket)
print(age >= 18 or has_ticket)
print(not has_ticket)

blocks.text: Each side must be a complete condition

blocks.caption: This prints even though x is 7:

blocks.text: Python reads this as **(x == 1) or (2)**. The left side is False, but the right side is just the number **2**, and every number except 0 counts as True. So the whole condition is always True.

blocks.wrong:
if x == 1 or 2:
    print("one or two")
blocks.right:
if x == 1 or x == 2:
    print("one or two")
blocks.why: Repeat the variable on both sides of **or**. Each side must be a full comparison.

blocks.caption: Or list the allowed values and use **in**:
blocks.code:
x = 7
print(x == 1 or x == 2)
print(x in (1, 2))

blocks.text: **x in (1, 2)** is True when x equals one of the values in the brackets. It is a short way to write a long chain of **or**.
Ranges

blocks.code:
x = 15
print(x >= 10 and x <= 20)
print(10 <= x <= 20)

blocks.text: Both lines mean "x is from 10 to 20". Python lets you chain the comparisons the way you would write them in maths.

blocks.wrong:
if x >= 10 or x <= 20:
    print("in range")
blocks.right:
if x >= 10 and x <= 20:
    print("in range")
blocks.why: Every number is at least 10 **or** at most 20, so the first version is True for every x, even 500. A range needs **and**.

blocks.text: Outside a range is the opposite: **x < 10 or x > 20**. That one needs **or**, because no number is below 10 and above 20 at the same time.
Short-circuit: Python stops as soon as it knows

blocks.code:
count = 0
total = 10
print(count != 0 and total / count > 2)

blocks.text: With **and**, if the left side is False the whole thing is False, so Python does not even look at the right side: the division by zero never happens. With **or**, if the left side is True, Python skips the right side.

blocks.caption: Swap the two sides and it crashes:
blocks.code:
count = 0
total = 10
print(total / count > 2 and count != 0)

blocks.text: Put the safety check first: **count != 0 and ...**, or **i < len(s) and s[i] == "x"**. The order of the two sides matters.
Flipping a combined condition

blocks.caption: When you flip, and becomes or, and or becomes and
rows: not both: at least one is False

blocks.code:
raining = False
cold = True
print(not (raining or cold))
print(not raining and not cold)

blocks.text: "Not (raining or cold)" describes a day that is neither raining nor cold. Both lines say exactly that.
Nested if, or and?

Both versions do the same. Use **and** when you only care about the case where both are True. Use a nested **if** when the inner check needs its own **else**, for example to print a different message for adults who are not members.

items: **and**: both. **or**: at least one. **not**: the opposite.
Each side of **and** and **or** is a full comparison: **x == 1 or x == 2**.
A range is **and** (or **10 <= x <= 20**); outside a range is **or**.
Python skips the right side once the answer is known, so put safety checks first.

lessons.title: Reading error messages
lessons.summary: Read the last line of a traceback, name the error, and know the usual cause of each common error.

blocks.text: Read a traceback from the **bottom**. The last line names the error and says what went wrong; the lines above it show where.

blocks.caption: A crash looks like this:
blocks.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(age + 1)
          ~~~~^~~
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

items: **Last line**: the error type, then a message in plain English.
**Line above it**: the exact code that failed.
**File ... line N**: where to look in your program.

blocks.caption: The errors you will meet most
rows: Python cannot read the code at all
a missing colon, bracket or quote, or = where you meant ==
the indentation does not match the blocks
nothing indented after a colon, or a line indented by accident
a typo, missing quotes around text, or using a variable before assigning it
this operation does not work on this type
the type is right, but not this value
s[len(s)], or s[0] on an empty string
this type has no method with that name

blocks.text: **SyntaxError** and **IndentationError** are found before anything runs, so not even the first line executes. The other errors happen while the program runs, at the line that fails; the lines before it have already run.

blocks.caption: A missing colon:
A block that is not indented:
blocks.output: IndentationError: expected an indented block after 'if' statement on line 1

blocks.caption: A method this type does not have:

blocks.text: Read the message literally: **'str' object has no attribute 'append'** means strings have no **append()** method. That one belongs to lists. Use **word + "!"** to build a longer string.

blocks.why: Without quotes **Hello** is read as a variable name, and there is no such variable, so this is a **NameError**, not a problem with print.

blocks.text: The error sometimes points at the line **after** the real mistake, for example when a bracket on the line above was never closed. If the reported line looks fine, check the one before it.

items: **TypeError**: the wrong type for this operation.
**ValueError**: the right type, but an impossible value.
**NameError**: an unknown name. Check the spelling and the quotes.
**IndexError**: a position past the end.
**AttributeError**: a method this type does not have, or a typo in its name.

steps.title: Ask Python for the type
steps.instructions: Type this program, then press **Run** and **Check**. **type(x)** tells you what kind of value **x** is, and **print()** shows the answer.

guide.explain: **42** is a whole number, so this prints **<class 'int'>**. Note the two closing brackets: one for **type(**, one for **print(**.
A number with a decimal point is a **float**.
Quotes make it text: **"42"** is a **str**, even though it looks like a number.
**True** (capital T, no quotes) is a **bool**.

print(type(42))
print(type(3.5))
print(type("42"))
print(type(True))

steps.instructions: Type this program. Only one branch runs: the **if** block when the condition is **True**, otherwise the **else** block.

guide.explain: Ask for the age as a whole number.
The condition ends with a colon. **age < 12** is either **True** or **False**.
Indented by 4 spaces: this line runs only when the condition is **True**.
**else** has no condition: it runs when the **if** condition was **False**.

tests.fail: With 15 it should print Adult ticket: 10 euros.

tests.name: 8 is a child
tests.fail: With 8 it should print Child ticket: 5 euros.

tests.name: 12 is an adult
tests.fail: With 12 it should print Adult ticket: 10 euros: 12 is not less than 12.

steps.title: Add a senior price
steps.instructions: People aged 65 or older pay less: **Senior ticket: 6 euros**. Add an **elif** between the **if** and the **else**.
hints: **elif age >= 65:** goes after the **if** block and before **else**.
**>=** means at least, so 65 itself counts.

tests.name: 70 is a senior
tests.fail: With 70 it should print Senior ticket: 6 euros.

tests.name: 65 is a senior
tests.fail: With 65 it should print Senior ticket: 6 euros: use >=.

tests.name: 64 is an adult
tests.fail: With 64 it should print Adult ticket: 10 euros.

tests.name: 5 is a child
tests.fail: With 5 it should still print Child ticket: 5 euros.

steps.title: Babies go free
steps.instructions: Children under 2 get in for free: **Free ticket**. Make sure an age of 1 gives **Free ticket**, not the child price. The order of the checks matters: only the first true branch runs.
hints: If **age < 12** comes first, a 1-year-old matches it and never reaches your new check.
Put **if age < 2:** first, and turn the old **if age < 12:** into an **elif**.

tests.fail: With 1 it should print Free ticket.

tests.name: 0 is free
tests.fail: With 0 it should print Free ticket.

tests.name: 2 is a child
tests.fail: With 2 it should print Child ticket: 5 euros.

tests.name: 70 is still a senior
tests.fail: With 70 it should still print Senior ticket: 6 euros.

steps.title: Positive, negative, even, odd
steps.instructions: On your own: ask for a whole number. Print **positive**, **negative** or **zero** on the first line, then **even** or **odd** on the second line.
hints: Two separate decisions, so two separate **if** statements.
A number is even when **n % 2 == 0**.
Use **==** to compare; a single **=** is a SyntaxError inside an if.

tests.fail: With 7: positive, then odd.
With -4: negative, then even.
With 0: zero, then even.
With -3: negative, then odd.

steps.title: Grade calculator
steps.instructions: Experiment: ask for a score. Print **A** for 90 or more, **B** for 80 or more, **C** for 70 or more, **D** for 60 or more, and **F** below that. A score above 100 or below 0 prints **Invalid score** instead.
hints: Check the invalid scores first, so 101 never gets an A.
Then go from the highest grade down: **elif score >= 90**, **elif score >= 80**, and so on.
Going from high to low means you never need an upper limit like **score < 90**.

tests.name: top grades
tests.code:
for typed, grade in [("95", "A"), ("90", "A"), ("89", "B"), ("80", "B")]:
    assert run_source(SOURCE, [typed]).strip() == grade, typed
tests.fail: 95 and 90 should give A; 89 and 80 should give B.

tests.name: lower grades
tests.code:
for typed, grade in [("70", "C"), ("69", "D"), ("60", "D"), ("59", "F"), ("0", "F")]:
    assert run_source(SOURCE, [typed]).strip() == grade, typed
tests.fail: 70 should give C, 69 and 60 D, 59 and 0 F.

tests.name: invalid scores
tests.code:
for typed in ["101", "-1", "250"]:
    assert run_source(SOURCE, [typed]).strip() == "Invalid score", typed
tests.fail: Scores above 100 or below 0 should print Invalid score and nothing else.

labs.title: Can you ride?
labs.summary: Combine conditions with and, or and not, fix the classic or bug, and write a leap year check.

steps.title: Tall enough and old enough
steps.instructions: Type this program. **and** is **True** only when both sides are **True**.

guide.code:
height = int(input("Height in cm? "))
age = int(input("Age? "))
guide.explain: Ask for the height and the age, both whole numbers.
Both conditions must hold. Each side is a full comparison.
One message for yes, one for no.

tests.name: 150 cm, 12
tests.fail: With 150 and 12: You can ride!

tests.name: 150 cm, 8
tests.fail: With 150 and 8: too young, so Sorry, not this time.

tests.name: 130 cm, 12
tests.fail: With 130 and 12: too short, so Sorry, not this time.

tests.name: 140 cm, 10
tests.fail: With exactly 140 and 10: You can ride!

steps.title: With an adult
steps.instructions: New rule: a child of at least **120** cm may also ride when an adult comes along. Ask a third question, **With an adult? (yes/no)**, and let them ride if (height at least 140 **and** age at least 10) **or** (height at least 120 **and** the answer is **"yes"**).
hints: Brackets make the two rules clear: **(rule one) or (rule two)**.
Compare the answer with **adult == "yes"**.
steps.solution:
height = int(input("Height in cm? "))
age = int(input("Age? "))
adult = input("With an adult? (yes/no) ")
if (height >= 140 and age >= 10) or (height >= 120 and adult == "yes"):
    print("You can ride!")
else:
    print("Sorry, not this time.")

tests.name: 130 cm, 8, yes
tests.fail: With 130, 8 and yes: You can ride!

tests.name: 130 cm, 8, no
tests.fail: With 130, 8 and no: Sorry, not this time.

tests.name: 110 cm, 8, yes
tests.fail: With 110, 8 and yes: still too short, Sorry, not this time.

tests.name: 150 cm, 12, no
tests.fail: With 150, 12 and no: You can ride! (the first rule still holds)

steps.title: Leap year
steps.instructions: On your own: ask for a year and print **Leap year** or **Not a leap year**. The rule: a year is a leap year when it is divisible by 4 and not by 100, or when it is divisible by 400.
hints: Divisible by 4 means **year % 4 == 0**; not divisible by 100 means **year % 100 != 0**.
Put the first rule in brackets: **(year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0) or year % 400 == 0**.
Test 1900 and 2000: they are the tricky ones.

tests.fail: 2024 is divisible by 4 and not by 100: Leap year.
2023 is not divisible by 4: Not a leap year.
1900 is divisible by 100 but not by 400: Not a leap year.
2000 is divisible by 400: Leap year.

steps.title: Divide safely
steps.instructions: Experiment with short-circuiting: ask for two whole numbers **a** and **b**. Print **Big** when **b** is not 0 and **a / b** is more than 10, otherwise **Small**. Use one **if** with **and**, so that **b = 0** never crashes.
hints: **and** stops as soon as the left side is **False**, so the right side is never worked out.
Put the safety check first: **b != 0 and a / b > 10**.
Swap the two sides and try **5** and **0**: you get a ZeroDivisionError.

tests.name: 100 and 5
tests.fail: 100 / 5 is 20, more than 10: Big.

tests.name: 100 and 20
tests.fail: 100 / 20 is 5: Small.

tests.name: 5 and 0
tests.fail: With b = 0 it should print Small without crashing.

tests.name: uses and
tests.fail: Combine the two checks with and in one condition.

labs.title: Fix the broken programs
labs.summary: Read each error message, find the line it points at, and fix one bug at a time.

steps.title: A program that works
steps.instructions: Type this program carefully, then **Run** and **Check**. Each explanation says which error you would get if you got that line wrong, so you know what to look for in the next steps.

guide.explain: **float()** turns the typed text into a number. Leave it out and line 3 gives a **TypeError**; use **int()** and typing 2.5 gives a **ValueError**.
Forget a closing bracket here and Python reports a **SyntaxError**.
Misspell **price** as **prise** and you get a **NameError**: Python has never seen that name.
Put spaces in front of this line and you get an **IndentationError**.

steps.solution:
price = float(input("Price? "))
count = int(input("How many? "))
total = price * count
print("Total:", total)

tests.fail: With 2.5 and 4 it should print Total: 10.0.

tests.name: 1.5 times 2
tests.fail: With 1.5 and 2 it should print Total: 3.0.

steps.title: Fix the TypeError
steps.instructions: This program should print **Next year you will be 18** for an age of 17. Run it, read the TypeError, and fix it.
steps.starter:

print("Next year you will be " + age + 1)

steps.title: Two bugs at once
steps.instructions: Experiment: this program has two bugs. It should print **Total: 5.0** for a price of **2.50** and a count of **2**. Fix the first error, run again, and fix the next one. Python stops at the first error, so you only see one at a time.
steps.starter:

count = int(input("How many? "))
print("Total: " + price * count)
hints: The first error is a **ValueError**: **int("2.50")** cannot read a decimal point. Which function can?
The second error is a **TypeError**: text plus a number. Use a comma in **print()**, or **str()**.
Read the last line of the error first: it names the kind of error and the line.

count = int(input("How many? "))
print("Total:", price * count)
